Find the total charge $Q$ of a metal plate that occupies the region $D$ enclosed between  the parts of  the curves ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ and ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ as shown above, and has charge density $\rho (x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that the region $D$ represents a half-annulus enclosed between the circles of the radiuses $1$ and $2$ centered at the origin.

The total charge $Q$ of an object occupying the region $D$ with charge density $\rho (x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}$ is given by

$$
Q={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}\rho (x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }\rho (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

The following equations connect Cartesian and polar coordinates:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain $r=2.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain $r=1.$

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}[r]_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(2-1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\, \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the object is $Q=\pi .$
